newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lower Buba reserves arouse intervention suspicion.
newsitem.headline: Lower Buba reserves arouse intervention suspicion.

text.p: A sharp decline in Bundesbank foreign currency reserve levels at the end of July has aroused market suspicion that the central bank may have been quietly intervening in currency markets to support the deutschemark.
The reserves, held mainly in dollars, were worth 118.8 billion marks ($62.9 billion) in the week ending June 7 and had been coming down in small steps, falling to 116.6 billion marks by July 23.
But in the seven days from July 23, the decline accelerated substantially with the level dropping sharply by 1.2 billion marks to leave reserves of 115.5 billion marks by July 31.
In its weekly report, the bank said the drop was due mainly to "Bundesbank transactions in which previous inflows of foreign currency from outside the market were disposed of".
A Bundesbank spokesman told Reuters these "inflows" were dollars which come to the central bank from U.S. institutions in Germany and which are then sold back into the market.
He declined to say what the bank had bought with the dollars, but said the operation was "nothing unusual".
Some market participants say the drop in reserves might be a sign that the central bank is selling dollars behind the scenes to support the ailing mark.
"It is certainly worth watching the reserve levels," said Michael Wallace, manager of European FX analysis at Standard and Poor's MMS in London.

"I have heard some talk that if the Bundesbank were intervening and selling dollars, it may be more subtle this time, with the bank just trying to slow things down and then let the market fall on its own sword."

The mark has been beaten lower against the dollar in recent months but the pace of its decline has stepped up a gear in the past few weeks with the German currency hitting its lowest level in eight years on Wednesday, just over 1.89 marks.
By 1345 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.8745 marks.

Speculation about whether the Bundesbank will defend the mark was heightened further on July 24 when the central bank declined to set a money market repurchase, or repo, agreement for the whole of its four-week holiday period.
The bank set a fixed 3.0 repo rate for two weeks but did not specify the type of agreement it would set for the second two holiday weeks. The summer break ends on August 21.

Some market players say it is possible that, by leaving its repo options open, the Bundesbank was trying to lure market attention away from talk of intervention and towards speculation about a move in the money market rate, leaving itself room to dabble in foreign exchange markets unnoticed.
But while analysts said the 1.2 billion reserve drop in the week to July 31 was large compared with recent weeks, they were not convinced this was anything out of the ordinary.

"It is a relatively high number," said Holger Fahrinkrug, economist at UBS in Frankfurt. "But if you look at the last week of July 1996 reserves were down 3.6 billion marks, so it is obviously something that happens occasionally."

In 1993, when severe tensions within the exchange rate mechanism (ERM) sent Europe floundering into currency crisis and the Bundesbank moved decisively to support neighbouring currencies by buying them against the mark, much larger swings were seen in the central bank's reserve levels.

In the week to August 12 1993, for example, the Bundesbank weekly report said reserves were bloated by 39.3 billion marks "as a result of renewed support operations within the boundaries of the European exchange rate mechanism".
Around a month later, the level dropped by 21.6 billion marks in one week, suggesting the bank was selling the currencies acquired through intervention back into the markets.
"Those are the kind of figures we saw when they really are intervening," said Fahrinkrug.

"They have occasionally in the past intervened with much smaller amounts, particularly when there is coordinated intervention, but that is the kind of move when central banks want to be seen in the headlines without shifting their currency positions too greatly."

In the current case, if the Bundesbank were making a bid to support the mark cheaply, they would want to ensure the action constituted a strong signal by letting markets know about it, Fahrinkrug said.
Wallace, too, said he did not think the central bank would engage in such a surreptitious move to defend the mark.
"The reason the markets are carrying on the way they are is because they don't believe there is a real threat (of the Bundesbank intervening to support the mark)," he said.
"I wouldn't see much advantage gain for the Bundesbank from just leaking dollars in these kind of amounts into the market." ($ = 1.888 German Marks)
